node.label: Joan Wallach Scott
node.description: Develops gender as a historical analysis of social relationships and power. Her 1986 formulation connects symbols, normative claims, institutions and subjectivity while insisting on historical variation.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis (1986).
node.scope_note: Existing cross-field presence warrants a visible argument, not just another name in a roster. This draft covers the 1986 intervention; later experience and secularism arguments need their own claims.

proposals.date_semantics: Selected work date, not career boundary or field origin.

record.context: Joint work questions a simple passage from unproductive domesticity to emancipating paid employment.
record.works: “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe” (1975); Women, Work, and Family (1978)

record.title: Work and family change
record.focus: Tilly and Scott question assumptions that women at home were unproductive and that wage work automatically meant emancipation.
record.works: 1975 joint article; Women, Work, and Family (1978)

record.context: Questions treating experience and social identities as self-evident foundations. Her intervention acknowledges recovery histories and retains experience as a historical problem to explain.
record.works: “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); “Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis” (1986)

record.title: Experience, identities and historical explanation
record.focus: Read Scott’s critique of foundational experience alongside Thompson’s historical class formation. Scott’s proposed historicization is not a consensus or a demand to abandon experience.
record.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

record.title: Experience, agency and changing discourse
record.focus: Canning accepts the need to historicize experience but questions treating identity recovery and analysis of difference as alternatives. She asks how subjects reinterpret or transform discourse; this is a sympathetic criticism of Scott, not a return to self-evident experience.
record.works: Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Canning (1994), 374–378

record.context: Questions treating experience as transparent evidence while retaining historical inquiry into how subjects are formed.
record.works: “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

record.title: Experience and exclusions
record.focus: Scott’s historical question and Crenshaw’s legal intervention challenge different ways of treating groups as homogeneous.
record.works: “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); “Demarginalizing…” (1989)

record.context: Treats gender and experience as historical questions, joining cultural and institutional interpretation.
record.works: “Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis” (1986); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

record.title: Gender, community and conflict
record.focus: Gender contributes to cultural inquiry and complicates unified pictures of communities and rituals.
record.works: Gender (1986); The Body Politic and Desan chapter (1989)

record.context: Historicizes gender categories and the production of experience while retaining institutional relations and historical inquiry.
record.works: “Gender” (1986); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

record.title: Signification and divided subjectivity
record.focus: Lacan’s changed sign diagram and reading of dream-work distinguish his appropriation from literal repetition of Saussure. Historians debate its capacity to explain changing gender relations.
record.works: “L’instance de la lettre” (1957); Scott, “Gender” (1986)

record.title: Gender categories and historical experience
record.focus: Scott makes experience something to explain and connects meanings with institutions and subjectivity.
record.works: Gender (1986); The Evidence of Experience (1991)

record.context: Gender as historical analysis.
record.works: Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis (1986)

record.title: Gender as historical analysis
record.focus: Scott’s relational account draws on named resources while distinguishing symbols, norms, institutions and subjective identity; it does not explain every approach in this umbrella.
record.works: Scott’s 1986 essay; feminist exchanges with Thompson

record.title: Psychoanalytic subjectivity and historical variation
record.focus: Scott values constructed subjectivity while questioning universal antagonism; her discussion of Alexander identifies a historical feminist use without establishing consensus.

record.title: Historicizing hierarchical oppositions
record.focus: Scott’s productive deconstructive use questions fixed binary hierarchies and calls for historical analysis; it is distinct from her criticism of universal psychoanalytic antagonism.
record.works: Scott, “Gender” (1986), p. 1066

record.context: Joint work joins family history to questions about productive work and historical change.

record.focus: Alice Clark’s earlier research, Tilly/Scott’s work-family inquiry and Anna Clark’s gendered class history have different questions and evidence.
record.works: Working Life (1919); Scott/Tilly (1975); Breeches (1995)

node.label: Natalie Zemon Davis
node.description: Uses contrasting seventeenth-century lives to investigate religion, writing and relations of power across Europe and its colonial outposts. Women on the Margins makes individual lives a route into broader historical questions.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995).
node.scope_note: Comparative biography provides a connection beyond gender history. This draft is supported by a newly checked book description; its methodological interpretation still needs a fresh body-text check. Other career contributions remain in the preserved contexts.

proposals.date_semantics: Selected work date, not career boundary or field origin.

record.context: Compares Glikl, Marie de l’Incarnation and Merian without making them one universal female trajectory. An explicitly imagined prologue tests her categories; stories, religious difference, colonial power and textual mediation shape interpretation.
record.works: Women on the Margins (1995), prologue, selected Glikl opening, conclusion and acknowledgments

record.title: Comparative lives, religion and colonial power
record.focus: Davis holds similarities and differences together, tests her categories through an imagined prologue and rejects a single progressive sequence. Marginality does not prevent participation in colonial domination.
record.works: Women on the Margins (1995), selected primary passages

record.title: Teaching, source discovery and collaborative work

record.works: Women on the Margins (1995), acknowledgments

record.context: Uses surviving writings to reconstruct three differently situated seventeenth-century lives.
record.works: Women on the Margins (1995)

record.title: Life histories and written lives

node.label: Lynn Hunt
node.description: Reassesses the explanatory models of social history in her introduction to The New Cultural History. She recognizes turns toward culture within Marxist and Annales histories while questioning the priority assigned to social experience.
node.scope_note: Connects the cultural turn to disputes within social explanation. Hunt authored this introduction and edited the collection; she did not author all its essays. Her political-culture work remains a separate inherited context.

node.label: Catherine Hall
node.description: With Leonore Davidoff, relates English middle-class formation to gender, family, religion and economic life in Family Fortunes. Class identities and gender relations are investigated together rather than in separate historical accounts.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class 1780–1850 (1987). Joint work; retain all coauthor credits.
node.scope_note: Equal coauthor credit with Davidoff. The 1987 work is distinct from Hall’s later introduction and later imperial history. Newly checked evidence is the indexed prologue abstract and publisher description of a later edition.

node.label: Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham
node.description: Argues that race structures the meanings of gender, class and sexuality. Her 1992 intervention challenges insufficient racial analysis in feminist theory and develops an account of race as socially constructed, contested power.
node.representative_figures_and_works: African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race (1992).
node.scope_note: A theoretical contribution within Black history as well as feminist historiography. Her opening acknowledges useful feminist resources and earlier Black scholarship; it does not license an indiscriminate critique edge to every cited theorist.

proposals.date_semantics: Selected work date, not career boundary or field origin.

node.label: Linda Tuhiwai Smith
node.description: Places research within colonial histories and Indigenous struggles over knowledge and self-determination. Decolonizing Methodologies addresses the responsibilities, community relationships and authority involved in research with Indigenous peoples.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Decolonizing Methodologies: Research and Indigenous Peoples (1999).
node.scope_note: Connects Indigenous historical authority with the politics of research. This is a situated methodological programme, not a claim that Indigenous research is uniform or that every Western method is rejected.

node.label: Lorraine Daston
node.description: With Peter Galison, investigates changing scientific ideals of objectivity through images and atlas-making. Their 1992 article distinguishes mechanical objectivity from other historically formed components of the concept.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Image of Objectivity (1992). Joint work; retain all coauthor credits.
node.scope_note: Adds a substantive history-of-science contribution beyond gender history. Galison retains equal authorship and argument credit. Their historical analysis does not assert that scientific objectivity is simply impossible.

record.title: Images and historical forms of objectivity
record.focus: Mechanical restraint is one historically situated ideal, distinct from a claim to truth or escape from every perspective.
record.works: The Image of Objectivity (1992)
